title: 人物传记 · Marie Curie · Day 16

questions.question: 居里拒绝为镭的提纯工艺申请专利、把方法完全公开。文章指出这一选择后来的实际结果是什么？
options: 别的公司抢先为同一工艺申请了专利，反过来禁止她的实验室继续提纯镭
各国实验室竞相提纯，镭价格很快大跌，肿瘤病人因此普遍用得起镭疗
公开没有回流：镭商照样高价卖镭，她自己反要靠募捐买实验用的镭
法国政府为表彰她的无私给予终身科研资助，居里一家从此再无经济之忧
questions.explanation: 文章借公共品博弈指出：她向公共池投了钱，镭商照样以十万美元一克出售，全家终身清贫。价格大跌、惠及病人是听起来顺理成章的结局，但文章记录的恰恰相反。
questions.question_en: Curie refused to patent her radium purification process and published it openly. What does the article say actually followed?
options_en: Another company patented the same process first and then barred her laboratory from continuing to purify radium
Labs worldwide raced to purify it, radium prices soon collapsed, and tumor patients could widely afford radium therapy
Openness had no way to flow back to her: dealers still sold radium at high prices, while she relied on donations to buy it
The French government rewarded her selflessness with lifelong research funding, and the family never wanted again
questions.explanation_en: Drawing on the public-goods game, the article notes she paid into the common pool, yet dealers still sold radium at $100,000 a gram while her family stayed poor. Falling prices and patient access sound like the natural ending, but the article records the opposite.

questions.question: 身边研究者陆续出现灼伤、贫血、早逝，居里仍坚持镭基本无害。文章认为这一盲区更深的根源是什么？
options: 她长期孤立于学界之外，没有任何渠道接触到同行陆续发表辐射损伤报告
她担心镭被证明有害会断送镭疗产业，让自己失去来自企业的经费和长期赞助
当时完全没有任何关于辐射危害的证据，任何科学家处在她的位置都会这样判断
她对镭近乎信仰式的投入，使承认它有害几乎等于否定她自己的身份与意义
questions.explanation: 文章说不能全推给时代，1900 年代已有同行因辐射受伤甚至死亡，证据并非完全缺席；根源是当一个发现成了你的身份，承认它有害就等于否定自己。破解之道是刻意制造外部视角。
questions.question_en: As colleagues suffered burns, anemia, and early deaths, Curie still insisted radium was essentially harmless. What does the article see as the deeper root of this blind spot?
options_en: She was long isolated from the scientific community and had no access to colleagues' reports on radiation injury
She feared proof of harm would kill the radium-therapy industry and cost her corporate funding and sponsorship
There was no evidence at all of radiation harm back then; any scientist in her position would have judged the same way
Her near-religious devotion to radium meant admitting its harm would amount to negating her own identity and meaning
questions.explanation_en: The article says it can't all be blamed on the era—by the 1900s colleagues had already been injured or killed, so evidence wasn't absent. The root is that once a discovery becomes your identity, admitting its harm means negating yourself; the remedy is deliberately seeking an outside view.
